First Missionary Journey
FURST MISH-uh-nair-ee JUR-nee
noun (church history / Acts)
From missionary, Latin mittere, to send; and journey, Old French journee, a day's travel. The term names the first recorded apostolic circuit of Acts 13—14.

📖 Biblical Definition

The First Missionary Journey is the gospel circuit of Acts 13—14, in which the Holy Ghost set apart Saul and Barnabas from the church at Antioch, saying, "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them" (Acts 13:2). Sent forth by the Spirit and commissioned by the laying on of the church's hands, they sailed to Cyprus, where Paul withstood the sorcerer Elymas and the deputy Sergius Paulus believed. Thence to Pisidian Antioch, where Paul preached Christ crucified and risen, and the Gentiles "were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord: and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed" (Acts 13:48). The Jews stirred up persecution at Iconium; at Lystra Paul healed a cripple, was hailed a god, then stoned and left for dead, yet rose and went on to Derbe. Returning, they confirmed the disciples and "ordained them elders in every church" (Acts 14:23). This journey displays the sovereign God thrusting forth His sent men, the gospel going to the Gentiles by definite election, and the planting of churches under a plurality of elders. This dictionary confesses that missions begin not in human enterprise but in the Spirit's commission through a sending church.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The first apostolic circuit, Acts 13—14, in which Paul and Barnabas, sent by the Holy Ghost from Antioch, carried the gospel through Cyprus and the cities of Asia Minor, planting churches and ordaining elders.

FIRST MISSIONARY JOURNEY, noun. The first recorded circuit of apostolic preaching, Acts 13 and 14, undertaken by Paul and Barnabas.

Begun at Syrian Antioch when the Holy Ghost said, "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them."

It compassed Cyprus, Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe, the gospel coming to the Gentiles.

It requires that messengers be sent by the Spirit through the church, and it forbids self-appointed mission apart from that commission.

Its end was churches confirmed and elders ordained, under the sanction of him who calls and sends.

📖 Key Scripture

Acts 13:2 — "As they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Ghost said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them."

Acts 13:48 — "And when the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord: and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed."

Acts 14:22 — "Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God."

Acts 14:23 — "And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the recurring danger is to sever missions from the local church and from sovereign election.

expand to see more

The chief abuse of this history is to read it as a charter for autonomous adventurism—men running before they are sent, accountable to no church, planting nothing that endures. But Luke is careful: the Spirit spoke within a worshipping congregation, the church fasted and laid on hands, and the apostles returned to report. The journey ends not with converts left to themselves but with elders ordained in every church. Missions is the church's work, extended through her sent men, not a freelance enterprise.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is that the success of the journey rested on God's decree: "as many as were ordained to eternal life believed." The same sovereign grace that hardened the gainsaying Jews opened the hearts of the Gentiles. Modern method-driven missiology, which trusts technique and numbers, must be answered by the Acts pattern—faithful preaching of Christ crucified, suffering borne with joy, and the planting of ordered churches, all under the hand of the God who calls.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The phrase joins Latin mittere (to send) with the journeys narrated in Acts 13—14.

expand to see more

Missionary derives from Latin mittere, missus, to send, mirroring the Greek apostello.

Journey comes through Old French journee, a day's travel or stage.

The Greek of Acts 13:2 reads aphorisate, "separate ye," the same root as set apart unto holiness.

Acts 13:3 uses apelusan, they sent away, after fasting, prayer, and the laying on of hands.

The pattern roots all true sending in the prior call and decree of the triune God.

Usage

"On the First Missionary Journey, Paul preached in the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch before turning to the Gentiles."

"The stoning of Paul at Lystra belongs to the First Missionary Journey, yet he rose and pressed on to Derbe."

"The First Missionary Journey closed with elders ordained in every church and a report given to the sending congregation at Antioch."
